title: Rohatsu Two Stories
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley sets two stories side by side during Rohatsu sesshin: the Buddha's enlightenment under the Bodhi tree and Wuzu's account of a puppet show. Eko tells how Mara attacks with fear, desire, and unworthiness, and how the Buddha touches the earth so that the arrows turn to flowers. Then Eko reads Wuzu's tale of calling out to the puppeteer behind the blue curtain and hearing, "Just watch the show. Why ask for names?" Eko follows the shifts from delight to the urge to explain to ideas overturned, and offers a bowl of oatmeal as a puppet show to stay loyal to.

As I settled in a little bit, I really appreciate more and more how beautiful all you are, particularly as you come into the practice rooms and put yourself out, step out into the public eye, perform your duties.
So thank you for being beautiful and thank you for showing that.
Well, I'd like to look at two stories today together, and one I think inevitably is the Enlightenment story.
Tim told part of that yesterday, but we need to get through it because we will be celebrating the culmination, so we need to have that in our minds a little bit.
And it is a heroic story, I think, no matter how you tell it.
We'll try to put some humanizing touches on it.
But I was thinking yesterday, what would it be like if we didn't have this heroic story?
It's kind of bothersome in a way, but what would our tradition be like if we didn't have this story at the center?

What if it was just some guy who just sort of slogged away for a while and through a lot of hard work came up with this teaching and went out and said, "Well, here, I've discovered this important thing."
But without that story, it seems to me it's a poor tradition.
That story, at least for me, draws me toward it in some way.
So I'd be interested to know how that is for other people.
I think for me it's like this bright light that I'm drawn toward.

So let's look at that story a little bit, the way I like to tell it, starting with Buddha's vow to sit under the Bodhi tree and not move until he gets to the bottom of human suffering and birth and death.
And whether he sits there for seven days or one night or seven years, it's not so important.

But any time we make a vow like that, and I think we've all made a vow somewhat in coming here this weekend, and we have a vow that's part of our practice, any time we really sort of articulate that to ourselves and the universe.
Maybe not any time, but often some challenges come up right away.
And I think psychologically it's not just accidental.
It's like we step into a new role and then all of our conditioning is activated to kind of say, "Oh no, we like the old way better," and so our own demons come forward.
Or perhaps it's something in our external life; often it's something internal.
So as you know in the story, Buddha sits down and through the long night Mara hears the vow and gets activated.
He's challenged by this, that somebody is going to get to the bottom of human suffering and find a better way to live this life.
He sort of relies on that to keep his little thing going.
And so he vows to knock Buddha off his seat.
And the first thing he does, according to my version of the story, is he tries to use fear.
And he assails Buddha with these fearsome images of arrows and warriors and demons and everything.
And Buddha remains upright.
He receives that energy without turning away, and the energy is dissipated.
So the arrows coming toward him turn into flowers.
And while this is sort of a fantastic image, we can experience something very similar.

And we can start on a little fear by just being present with it, allowing it to be there, and see how the energy that's contained in that complex or whatever you call it, just sort of dies away and is released.
So the next thing Mara does is desire.
And usually for a Buddha, it's depicted as young maidens, but whatever your strongest desire is, you can plug that into the story.
And again, Buddha is unmoving.
And again, the objects of desire sort of lose their energy, lose their attractiveness, from that simple act of being present with them, and in this case, not grasping.
And then finally, Mara's ultimate weapon is playing on Buddha's fears and our fears that we are not worthy, that we aren't good enough.
And so he whispers in Buddha's ear.
And what Buddha does then is touch the earth, and that famous mudra.
I think we have it up here, but often statues are depicted in that.
And the earth bears witness.
And for me, that is Buddha connecting with all beings.
And Buddha together with all beings are more than a match for Mara.
So Buddha is discovering and declaring that he can't do it alone.
And I think we can relate to that as well.
But there is this heroic aspect to it.
It's like fear and desire, feelings and unworthiness are vanquished forever, vanished from the scene.
And that is the part that is that shining ideal and doesn't seem to fit with our experience, although we can always hope that that will happen, it might, tonight.
But I think it's this other thing.
I think it's not something that we direct our practice toward, but it's something that we allow to inspire us in a different way.
There's a line that one encounters often in the polytext that has this sort of finality, final vanquishing to it.
And it always sort of rubs me the wrong way, but it has a certain hypnotic sound to it.
The line, "As birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived.
What had to be done has been done.
There's no more coming back to any state of being.
The holy life has been lived.
What needed to be done has been done," and we're kind of done with the whole thing.
And our practice, our Mahayana tradition and certainly Dogen's tradition, does not have that final vanquishing, at least not in anywhere near this way.
But again, I ask you to ponder what would it be like if we just eliminated this story and it had never been part of the tradition.
It's kind of interesting to think about.
So I'd like to tell a different story that is kind of a counterpoint to the heroic enlightenment story.
And this is a story about Utsu, who is in the Linji Rinzai line of Zen.
He's about the twentieth generation from Bodhidharma.
He appears several times in the Gateless Barrier.
So I was working on a koan there and looked him up in Andy Ferguson's book and there's other stories about him.
And I was immediately taken with the story.
In a lot of stories it's like, "Well, what does that mean?"
This story was just kind of delightful right from the beginning for me.
So let me read it to get it right.
It's very short.
Utsu addressed the monks, saying, "Yesterday, when I went into town, I noticed a puppet show going on.
I couldn't help going over there and taking a look.
The puppet was really something to see.
At first, it seemed to move its limbs, walk around and sit down all on its own.
But when you looked closer, you could see that there was someone behind the blue curtain.
I couldn't help but call out, 'Sir, what's your name?' The man replied, 'Honored priest, just watch the show.
Why ask for names?' Brethren, when I heard him say this, I didn't have a single word to say, nor a single idea to espouse.
Can any of you say anything in my place?"
Yesterday, that single instance of embarrassment has uprooted all my ideas.
So not so heroic, right?
Maybe a little more something we can relate to.
But there's a lot there, nevertheless.
So these are both encounter dialogues.
Most koans are encounter dialogues.
And we can see our practice, particularly the practice of sesshin, as one encounter after another, with a situation, with a thought, with a sensation, with a person, with a form.
And so these are examples of how different ways of responding to these encounters and following up from there.
Oops, I just put my thumb in my teeth.
So let's look at the story a little more carefully.
First line or two says, "Yesterday, when I went into town, I noticed a puppet show going on.
I couldn't help going over there and taking a look.
The puppet was really something to see."
So it's so unabashed, right?
And he sees this and he's kind of delighted to have this puppet show, and he expresses that.
And he says, "I couldn't help going over there and taking a look."
And that was okay, probably.
So imagine, if you will, you're outside on Fourth Street.
In the next moment the circus started coming down the street, you know, with the jugglers and the guys on stilts, the tigers and the dragons and the elephants that we read about in the pukanzazengi.
After sitting for a day and we were able to witness that, wouldn't that be delightful?
Wouldn't you want to run to the window and take a look at that?
Yes, yes.
So this is a nice story.
It's about delight, and we don't talk about that too much in this practice.
So he was clearly delighted.
And then things start to shift a little bit.
At first sight it seemed to move its limbs, walk around, sit down all on its own.
But when you looked closer you could see there was someone behind the blue curtain.

So in Zen stories when we're presented with sort of an illusory reality and another one behind a veil, our mind starts working and thinking, "Okay, there's a metaphor here," and, you know, "Is this like some sara or relative world and the absolute relative truth, the absolute truth?"
But we can set that aside.
I mean, you can ponder that.
But in the more immediate aspect of the story, would you just notice that there was a puppet master and he was doing things?
And maybe, you know, maybe you could still be delighted with that, right?
I mean, you don't have to, your mind doesn't have to shift necessarily, "Oh, there's another reality."
"Oh, it's a puppet show and something else," you know, "How wonderful."
But Utsu couldn't help but call out, "Sir, what's your name?
Give me a name.
How do you do that?
What's going on there?
This is so wonderful.
I want to know how you do it."
And he couldn't help it again, right?
And we already know that he's telling a story on himself, right?
So that kind of warms us up.
It's a nice stance for a teacher to take, I think.
And at this point, it looks like he's maybe slipped away from his initial delight a little bit.
And he's asking for names and explanations.
And please, you know, tell me how this is working here.
And so you might say that at this point, the world of suffering is born.
And you know, you can read the story various ways, but this one works.
So we have our delight.
We have our immediate experience.
And we start, then we slip off that and say, "Oh, you know, what's going on here?
I'd like a name for this and this, please."
And then we've created another layer.
We've created, we've unleashed our desire to manage and understand.
And perhaps at that point, the world of suffering is born.
The world of suffering is born.
So then this presence behind the blue curtain, it speaks, right?
So that's pretty amazing because we don't know who this is, right?
It's just something happening behind the blue curtain.
The man replied to me, "Honored priest, just watch the show.
Why ask for names?"
So just watch the show.
Just enjoy the show.
Just be engaged by the show.
Honored practitioners, why ask for names and explanations?
So Buddha had his show too, right?
I mean, Mara, Mara was the puppet master.
Put on the displays and Buddha was very upright.
And he allowed the show to sort of dissipate.
Utsu is, he's delighted by the show, and so he gets involved in the show, which I don't think is a bad thing.
But then asking for names, again, that's another part of the show in some ways.
But we ask for explanations and we slip away.
Then again, the show is anything.
The show is the moving behind the curtain.

The show is anything that's included in our vivid immediate experience before we yell out and ask for names and explanations, conceptual frameworks and reasons, which are good, but they create some problems for us.
Brethren, when I heard him say this, I didn't have a single word to say in reply, nor a single idea to espouse.
So it's like Buddha comes back from the grave, right?
And he's behind the blue curtain now.
And he's saying, "Honored practitioners, just enjoy the show, please.
And don't ask for names."
And Utsu was brought up short.
And, you know, he didn't, he sort of realized it.
Didn't start making excuses.
He allowed it to change him.
And he was a teacher and maybe needed to espouse an idea from time to time, but there was nothing appropriate here.
Espousing ideas was beside the point.
And one reason I like this story is I can kind of feel each of the shifts, right?
I can relate to that, and maybe you can too.
The first, the delight, "Oh yeah."
And then the mind noticing something that sort of slides into, "Well, oh, how does that work?"
And then the slipping away.
And maybe something from the teaching arises, "Well, okay, return to the, return to your breath."
"Oh, okay," or simply let go.
And all the ideas that I've been carrying with me about sesshin or about practice.
If I am, if I've been sitting for a day and a half, right, then perhaps they're all overturned, which is scary, but very, very fertile happening.
And he asks us, "Can any of you say anything in my place?"
It's like, "What if you were there?"
I mean, you can relate to this, can't you?
He's not bettering the assembly or even challenging them, I think.
He's saying, "Can't you see how that was?
What would you have done?
Yesterday, that single instance of embarrassment has uprooted all my ideas now."
He's coming before the assembly and really saying, "I have nothing more to say.
I have nothing more to say.
My ideas have all been overturned."
It's interesting to notice which of these stories we want our teacher to embody and which of them we want ourselves to embody.
It's kind of a tricky thing.
I think this heroic story is inspiring, and sometimes we would really like our teacher to be that hero because we can relate to that, and then maybe we will be too, you know that?
There is an aspect of that in our practice.
There is the aspect of Buddha experience of liberation.
Various teachers throughout the tradition have experienced the liberation, and that liberation is held out and said, "You too can experience liberation."
But this other archetype, this other model is also, I think, very important in our age.

I think it creates a lot fewer problems when we use this kind of model to see our teacher through and see our own practice through, and allow the expression of humility and delight and fascination and ideas overturned to be the teaching and to be our practice.
So Utsu is refusing to carry any projections about perfection and heroism.
Utsu is saying, "No, that's not me.
See the kind of thing that happens to me."
And yet he is a very strong teacher.
So I think there are several things we can take from this and use in our practice for the rest of shin and onward.
And one I would like to phrase as a loyalty to our immediate experience.
And the loyalty, I've been using that word lately, but it's, you know, we're so loyal to our self that wants and doesn't want, and it's this project that we carry around with us, right?
And we're very loyal to it.
But to have some faith that that's not the whole thing, of course, and that our true heart lies elsewhere.
And it's through this immediate experience.
Perhaps that is the gateway.
And so that immediate experience, while it seems somewhat separate from the me project, it is very much who we are.
It is very much, it is deeply, truly who we are.
That shifting our loyalty a little bit, saying, "Okay, I'm actually going to choose this with a lighter heart.
Choose this immediate experience."
It's not something that, it's not only something that the teaching says I should do, but I recognize something about that, that vivid aliveness.
So I'm going to begin to choose that more often and choose it more willingly.
And notice how that loyalty kind of switches back and forth.
So when presented with, you know, a bowl of oatmeal, it's a puppet show, "How fascinating," or "How delightful," or "How, at least how vivid it can be."
And we don't need to, as Tim was saying, we don't need to slip into preferences about seasoning or amounts or the whole who knows what.
We can stick with that vivid, immediate experience.
And as we do that in sesshin like this, I think you may well find, if you haven't already, that your ideas do get overturned.
A couple of people have mentioned in practice meetings, "It's like, I don't know why I'm here anymore.
I had this, you know, it was very clear, but now it's like, what is this all about?"
And I think that's a fertile time, not something to be avoided.
And again, there's a vivid experience that one can not need to name, not need to manage.
So as we go into the rest of the day and the night and tomorrow morning's celebration, it's pretty simple, isn't it, right?
Just stay with our vivid experience and allow the container of sesshin to take care of the things that need being taken care of.
And notice when we slip away from that vividness and ask for names and explanations, why's and wherefores.
And simply come back, notice how our ideas are, if not overturned, at least shaken up a little bit.
And we can hold onto them more lightly or simply let them go entirely.
And of course there is, in that being present with the vividness, it's not only delight, but it's kindness.
And softness and the refraining from wanting to explain is another face of that kindness.
And I look forward to the rest of this event, practicing with you in this beautiful tradition, in this beautiful way.
Thank you.
